blocks.text: Many scholars read the chapter as a symbolic review of Persian and Hellenistic conflicts whose correspondence becomes especially close in the account of Antiochus IV. On this reading, the description of the ruler’s end diverges from what is known of Antiochus’s death, so the chapter should not be forced into a harmony that hides the difference. This approach also distinguishes Daniel’s sixth-century narrative setting from scholarly proposals about the formation of its tales, visions, collection, and final form. The “abomination that maketh desolate” in verse 31 is understood in this horizon as referring to an Antiochene desecration of the temple, while later Jewish and Christian reuses of the phrase should be identified as later reuses rather than merged into the same event.

Reading Daniel 11 with its close historical correspondences and its final divergence in view can keep interpretation candid about both its precision and its limits. The chapter’s apocalyptic hope may be read as resistance to imperial domination, but that resistance does not supply a single required response for faithful people. Interpretations that intensify conspiracy, end-times fear, authoritarian control, nationalism, war, or genocide run against responsible safeguards for reading apocalyptic material.
